alt: Timeline of the occupation of Zimbabwe: Berlin Conference 1884-85, Grobler Treaty 1887, Moffat Treaty February 1888, Rudd Concession 30 October 1888, Royal Charter to the British South Africa Company 29 October 1889 and the Pioneer Column reaching Fort Salisbury on 12 September 1890.
caption: Figure: key dates from the Berlin Conference to the Pioneer Column (not to scale)

alt: Timeline from the Lancaster House constitution to 2013: conference and agreement of 21 December 1979, independence on 18 April 1980, reserved seats abolished and executive presidency in 1987, Senate abolished 1990, draft rejected February 2000, Senate brought back 2005, Global Political Agreement 2008 and COPAC from 2009, referendum approval 16 March 2013 and signing on 22 May 2013.
caption: Figure: from Lancaster House to the 2013 Constitution (not to scale)

alt: Timeline of the First Chimurenga: rising in Matabeleland from March 1896, in Mashonaland from June 1896, Matabeleland fighting largely ended after the 1896 indabas in the Matobo Hills, Mashonaland resistance continued into 1897 and Nehanda and Kaguvi were executed in April 1898.
caption: Figure: key dates of the First Chimurenga, 1896 to 1898 (not to scale)

alt: Timeline of Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa state: Great Zimbabwe grew from the 1100s and was at its height between about 1300 and 1450 CE, the Mutapa state was founded in the fifteenth century in northern Zimbabwe, and Great Zimbabwe became a World Heritage Site in 1986.
caption: Figure: approximate dates for Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa state (not to scale)

alt: Hierarchy of indigenous leaders from top to bottom: king or paramount ruler (mambo, inkosi), chief (ishe, inkosi or induna), headman (sadunhu, induna of a smaller area) and village head (sabhuku), each with its own area and roles.
caption: Figure: the hierarchy of indigenous leaders, from king to village head

alt: Timeline of the Second Chimurenga: UDI on 11 November 1965, Battle of Chinhoyi 28 April 1966, Altena Farm 21 December 1972, Nyadzonia 9 August 1976, Chimoio 23 November 1977, Freedom Camp 19 October 1978, Lancaster House Agreement signed 21 December 1979 and independence on 18 April 1980.
caption: Figure: key dates of the Second Chimurenga, 1965 to 1980 (not to scale)

alt: The three arms of government under the 2013 Constitution: the Executive (Chapter 5: President, Vice-Presidents, Cabinet and civil service), the Legislature (Chapter 6: Parliament, made up of the Senate and National Assembly) and the Judiciary (Chapter 8: judges and magistrates headed by the Chief Justice); each checks the others.
caption: Figure: the three arms of central government and their main functions

alt: Schematic map of Zimbabwe's five World Heritage Sites, not to scale: Victoria Falls (natural, 1989) on the Zambezi in the north-west, Mana Pools, Sapi and Chewore (natural, 1984) in the Middle Zambezi valley, Khami (cultural, 1986) near Bulawayo, Matobo Hills (cultural, 2003) south of Bulawayo and Great Zimbabwe (cultural, 1986) near Masvingo.
caption: Figure: where Zimbabwe's five World Heritage Sites lie (schematic, not to scale)
